transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-12
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~62 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CTO - Orion Cloud), Marcus Hill (Lead ML Eng), Priya Desai (Infra)

Summary: Technical deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy. Focus on cache key design, multi-tenant safety, hit-rate expectations, latency/throughput tradeoffs, KV cache sizing, batching interactions, quantization impacts, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Action items and pilot next steps agreed.

Topics: prefix caching, KV cache hit rates, cache keys, multi-tenant isolation, cache eviction policies, batching/throughput, quantization, VPC/on-prem security, metrics to capture

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, appreciate it. we wanted to zoom in on prefix caching, and really the operational tradeoffs if you were to run this in dedicated or private deployments.
[00:18] Lena Ortiz: yeah thanks, Maya. this is top of mind for us. we've got a lot of repeating system prompts and onboarding prefixes, so the potential cost savings are big, but we need to understand correctness and safety.
[00:30] Samir Patel: great, quick toggles: i'll run through how our KV/prefix cache works today, hit rates we've seen in other customers, and then we can map that to your workload. just flagging i might mis-say a few product names, apologies in advance.
[00:44] Marcus Hill: all good. also we care a lot about tail latency — can't have cache misses causing 500ms+ spikes.
[00:52] Samir Patel: understood. so at a high level: Redwood's prefix-caching stores the encoded KV cache state for a prefix chunk — that can be a system prompt, user profile chunk, or a conversation segment. when a request arrives, we check the cache key derived from a canonicalized prefix signature. if it's a hit we hydrate the KV cache into the runtime and skip the prefix tokens' attention computation.
[01:15] Lena Ortiz: can you explain the cache key canonicalization? this is one of our big concerns because we have slight variations of prompts between tenants.
[01:24] Samir Patel: yeah. keys are built from a few components: model id + model version hash + normalized prefix text fingerprint + optional tenant scoping token. normalization does whitespace collapse, placeholder substitution for PII, and stable ordering for templated fields. we also have an optional transformation step that applies language-agnostic canonicalization — that helps with small paraphrases. caveat: paraphrase normalization helps but isn't bulletproof.
[01:52] Priya Desai: and tenant scoping token — is that per-customer only, or do you do per-workspace?
[01:58] Samir Patel: you can scope at whichever granularity: global (disabled), customer, workspace, or route. for multi-tenant hosted customers we default to per-customer scoping to avoid cross-tenant leakage. in Dedicated/Private you pick what maps to your tenancy model.
[02:12] Marcus Hill: how do you guard against key collisions — two different prefixes mapping to same fingerprint?
[02:18] Samir Patel: it's rare but possible. we use 256-bit keyed fingerprinting (not plain MD5) with a salt tied to the model version; collisions are basically negligible. we also version the cache entries and keep a small audit trail so if something odd happens you can invalidate by prefix id.
[02:35] Lena Ortiz: ok. let's talk hit rates: what should we expect for a product like ours — lots of onboarding flows and templated responses but also lots of user-specific data.
[02:46] Samir Patel: from customers with similar patterns, raw hit rates on canonicalized prefixes range 40-65% for the first-turn system prompts and 20-40% for multi-turn conversation segments. critical lever is how you template and replace volatile tokens (user ids, timestamps). more templating = higher hit rate. we also see cumulative savings on token compute of 30-60% depending on prefix length distribution.
[03:15] Marcus Hill: do those hit rates assume in-memory hot LRU caches across multiple GPUs or a shared remote redis-like store?
[03:22] Samir Patel: good call. the numbers I quoted are for a hybrid approach: hot in-node memory for the most frequent prefixes + a sharded remote cache (rocksdb or redis) for warm entries. in Dedicated we run the remote cache on local SSDs for lower latency. in Private/On-prem we recommend colocated instance-local stores to avoid network roundtrips.
[03:44] Priya Desai: what about eviction policies? we can't let the cache grow unbounded across tenants.
[03:50] Samir Patel: we have hierarchical eviction: per-tenant quotas, LFU+time-decay heuristics, and a global cap. entries are charged by compressed KV state size. you can set hard caps per tenant and a soft cap that triggers more aggressive eviction. plus an LRU hotlist for in-memory nodes.
[04:06] Lena Ortiz: and multi-tenant safety — will a tenant ever read a KV state that originated from another tenant?
[04:13] Samir Patel: never in our design: all cache keys include tenant scope unless you explicitly opt-out. even for shared model ids we namespace keys with tenant id. in managed-hosted we also encrypt entries at rest and use KMS to bind keys to tenant scope.
[04:27] Lena Ortiz: we will need that on the SOC2 scope. also audit logs for cache hits and misses per-tenant.
[04:34] Maya Chen: yep we have an audit trail which logs key hashes and event metadata (no raw prefix text stored in logs unless you opt-in). for SOC2 we can provide the doc appendix — we'll share that as an action item.
[04:46] Marcus Hill: curious about the cost vs latency tradeoff. if we increase cache lookup depth or do a remote lookup, do we risk increasing median latency? how do you balance?
[04:57] Samir Patel: lookup is a lightweight signature compute + hash lookup; local memory lookups are sub-ms. remote lookups depend on network; for remote we co-locate and keep warm entries local. if a prefix is cold and we pull from remote, that can add 10-30ms depending on topology — still far less than re-computing 1k tokens. the tricky bit is when eviction causes a spike of misses; we mitigate by prefetch heuristics for high-frequency routes and by adaptive batching.
[05:25] Priya Desai: speak to prefetch heuristics?
[05:27] Samir Patel: we watch route-level request patterns and pre-warm the KV cache for prefixes that have a high short-term forecast. we can also pin certain prefixes as non-evictable (e.g., confirm screens). pinning is disabled by default but available in Dedicated/Private.
[05:45] Lena Ortiz: how does batching interact with prefix caching? our peak throughput requires big micro-batches.
[05:50] Samir Patel: batching and prefix caching are complementary. if you have many requests sharing a prefix, batching amplifies the benefit — you hydrate once and serve many. the runtime supports simultaneous hydration into the GPU KV cache then runs token generation across the batch. careful scheduling is needed to keep memory fragmentation low; we do continuous batching with memory-aware packing.
[06:10] Marcus Hill: quantization — if we use Q4 or Q5 models, does the KV cache remain compatible across quantization levels?
[06:17] Samir Patel: the KV tensor layout can differ between quantized and full-precision runtimes, so cache entries are versioned by kernel/quantization profile. you can't reuse a cached KV generated under one quantization profile with another. we recommend pinning the quantization profile for the rollout period if you want stable cache reuse.
[06:36] Lena Ortiz: so if we plan to A/B quantize between routes, we'd have much lower reuse across variants.
[06:41] Samir Patel: correct, reuse drops if quant profiles differ. you can still share prefixes within the same quant bucket. we also offer a lightweight shim that stores a canonicalized attention snapshot that is slightly larger but more format-agnostic — tradeoff is storage overhead.
[06:57] Priya Desai: encryption — you mentioned entries are encrypted at rest. in on-prem we want HSM/KMS integration and the ability to rotate keys without invalidating the entire cache. is that possible?
[07:06] Samir Patel: yes. we support envelope encryption with customer-managed KMS/HSM. key rotation is supported via dual-write of metadata; we maintain a small compatibility window where entries encrypted under an old key are readable while we re-encrypt lazily. you can also opt for a forced re-encrypt at maintenance window.
[07:22] Lena Ortiz: good. for VPC/private, what's the recommended network topology to avoid extra hops on cache lookup?
[07:29] Samir Patel: recommended: colocate cache shards on the same subnet as the inference nodes; use a local load-balancer to route requests; avoid crossing AZs for cache hot path. in Private installs we deploy sidecars that expose a unix-socket path for local lookups to cut latency.
[07:45] Marcus Hill: instrumentation — what metrics should we capture to evaluate pilot success?
[07:50] Samir Patel: key metrics: prefix cache hit rate (per-route and global), token compute saved (tokens avoided), median and 95/99 tail latency pre/post caching, cache miss cost (latency and compute), cache churn rate, and per-tenant cache storage usage. also an SLO for incorrect reuse (should be zero) and audit log counts.
[08:14] Lena Ortiz: what about correctness regressions — e.g., if a cached prefix was created under a model variant that had a subtle instruction-following bug — how do we detect/regress?
[08:24] Samir Patel: two parts: you can bind cache entries to model version hashes; if you detect a regression you can invalidate by model-hash. additionally, Redwood Evaluate can run a small canary eval on precached responses vs live generation to detect quality regressions; we can include that in the pilot.
[08:41] Priya Desai: capacity planning — what's the storage footprint per cached prefix roughly? we have lots of 300–800 token prefixes.
[08:49] Samir Patel: KV size varies by model/seq length; rough ballpark: 300-token prefix -> ~40–80 KB compressed for Llama-like models when storing key+value tensors compressed; 800-token prefix -> 120–250 KB. these are approximate. we recommend a conservative per-tenant cap and metrics to watch during pilot.
[09:12] Marcus Hill: that means storage could grow quickly. we should set a soft cap and TTL.
[09:16] Lena Ortiz: agreed. let's talk about benchmarking. what does your benchmark harness look like?
[09:21] Samir Patel: we have a harness that replays traffic with synthesized slight variations (timestamp/user ids templated) and measures hit rates and end-to-end latency. for the pilot we'd ask for a one-day sample (anonymized) to simulate. we also run a 1k-request burst test to surface tail behaviors.
[09:40] Maya Chen: important operational note — we don't store raw prefix text in the cache unless you opt-in; only fingerprints and encrypted state. we can provide the exact schema in the design doc.
[09:50] Lena Ortiz: good. one more question: can caching ever change semantics — e.g., prompt that depends on external context like live user status?
[09:58] Samir Patel: yes, if the prefix includes live state that changes frequently, caching might cause stale outputs. Solution: use short TTLs for those entries, or incorporate a dynamic context marker into the key (e.g., user_status_version). we recommend cataloging which prefix segments are stable vs volatile during onboarding.
[10:18] Marcus Hill: any production pitfalls to watch for? we've seen miss storms during deployments before.
[10:23] Samir Patel: common pitfalls: wrong normalization (over-collapsing distinct prompts), eviction mis-tuning causing mass misses, and mixing quant profiles. mitigation: start conservative, enable per-route telemetry, run chaos/eviction tests, and run a canary rollout. we have rollout helpers that drain and repopulate caches gradually.
[10:43] Priya Desai: security review side: will you need network egress to Redwood managed control plane during pilot?
[10:49] Maya Chen: for Private/VPC we can run fully air-gapped except for initial license activation and optional telemetry. for Dedicated we do control-plane calls over TLS but data path stays in customer VPC. we'll detail these deployment modes in the appendix.
[11:05] Lena Ortiz: ok sounds good. recap next steps?
[11:08] Maya Chen: recap: Samir runs benchmarks and shares results by 11/19; Maya shares design doc + security appendix by 11/14; Priya provides traffic/exemplar prefixes by 11/17; schedule pilot kickoff 11/24.
[11:20] Marcus Hill: and during the pilot we'll capture the metrics you listed and run the canary evals for quality.
[11:27] Samir Patel: i'll add a small checklist in the benchmark results: hit rate, token savings, tail latency delta, storage per-prefix, and any abnormal collisions or mis-hits.
[11:36] Lena Ortiz: thanks everyone. we feel good about cautious pilot approach.
[11:40] Maya Chen: awesome, thanks all. we'll follow up with calendar invite and docs.

End of transcript.
